# Isometries and gauge fields {#sec-nonabelian-isometries}

Kaluza's fifth dimension produced one gauge field, the photon, because the circle has one symmetry: the rotation
generated by the Killing vector $\partial_y$ (Part III, @sec-kk-gauge). The Standard Model needs twelve gauge fields
and three non-commuting gauge groups, and the natural question, first asked by DeWitt, is whether a larger internal
space with a larger symmetry group can produce them all from geometry. This chapter answers the first half of the
question. Replacing the circle by an internal space with a non-abelian group of isometries, the sphere $S^2$ with its
three rotations being the running example, the off-diagonal components of the metric become one gauge field per
Killing vector, and the coordinate changes along the Killing vectors become Yang-Mills gauge transformations whose
structure constants are those of the isometry algebra.

The chapter has two sections. The first, on the ansatz, recalls the Killing vectors of the internal space (Part I,
@sec-flows-killing), writes the non-abelian Kaluza-Klein ansatz on $M_4 \times M_k$ and inverts it; the inverse is a
statement about block matrices that holds for every internal space at once. The second derives the gauge
transformation from the Lie derivative of the metric along spacetime-dependent isometries and identifies the gauge
algebra with the opposite of the Killing algebra, the Lie algebra of the isometry group of @sec-lie-groups-algebras.
The geometric picture behind both is that of a fibre bundle with structure group $G$ (@sec-fibre-bundles), and the
sphere is the simplest coset space $SO(3)/SO(2)$ of @sec-coset-spaces. The next chapter reduces the curvature scalar
and meets the consistency problem. Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden
solutions.

## Isometries as gauge symmetries: the ansatz {#sec-nonabelian-ansatz}

Replacing the circle by a sphere replaces the single Killing vector $\partial_y$ by the three Killing vectors of
$SO(3)$, and the single gauge field by three: the gauge group of the reduced theory is the isometry group of the
internal space. This section sets up the non-abelian Kaluza-Klein ansatz on $M_4 \times S^2$, the sphere of Part I
as $SO(3)/SO(2)$, following @duff1994 [Sec. 5] and @overduin1998 [Sec. 4.3]; its block inverse holds for an
arbitrary internal space.

### Internal isometries

The ansatz needs two ingredients from the internal space: a metric that fixes its size and shape, and the Killing
vectors that generate its symmetries. The definition collects both and fixes the sign with which the internal metric
enters the higher-dimensional metric of signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-internal-isometries}
#### Internal space with isometries

An **internal space** is a compact Riemannian manifold $(M_k, \gamma)$ with positive-definite metric $\gamma_{mn}(y)$ and a
group $G$ of isometries generated by Killing vectors $K_a = K^m_a\partial_m$ (@def-killing), $a = 1, \dots, \dim G$, closing into the
Lie algebra of $G$, $[K_a, K_b] = f_{ab}{}^cK_c$ (@def-isometry-algebra). The compactification is $M_4 \times M_k$, and
the Kaluza-Klein ansatz couples the Killing vectors to gauge fields on $M_4$. Inside the full metric the internal
block is $h_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$, so that $\hat g$ has signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$ (@sec-conventions-indices); the
geometry of $M_k$ itself, its Killing vectors and its curvature $R_\gamma$, is that of the positive metric $\gamma$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The round two-sphere is the example the whole of this Part returns to. Its three Killing vectors were found in Part I,
and their brackets fix the structure constants that will reappear in the gauge transformation.

::: {#exm-internal-sphere}
#### The sphere

$S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$ with the round metric $d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ and the three Killing vectors
@eq-sphere-killing, $K_1 = -\sin\varphi\,\partial_\theta - \cot\theta\cos\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$, $K_2 = \cos\varphi\,\partial_\theta -
\cot\theta\sin\varphi\,\partial_\varphi$, $K_3 = \partial_\varphi$, with $[K_a, K_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}K_c$ (@eq-killing-brackets,
@prp-killing-brackets): $f_{ab}{}^c = -\epsilon_{abc}$, the algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ (@exr-s2-killing-algebra).
:::

The circle of Part III is the degenerate case with a one-dimensional abelian isometry group. Keeping it in view checks
every formula of this chapter, because each must reduce to its Part III counterpart.

::: {#exm-internal-circle}
#### The circle

$S^1$ with $\gamma = \phi^2$ ($h = -\phi^2$) and the single Killing vector $K = \partial_y$, $f = 0$: the ansatz of @sec-kk-ansatz is the
case $\dim G = 1$, and every formula below reduces to Part III when $K^m_a = 1$.
:::

Flat tori and group manifolds show that the number of Killing vectors is not tied to the dimension of the space. A
torus has as many as dimensions, a group manifold twice as many, and a coset as many as the group that acts on it.

::: {#exm-internal-torus-group}
#### Tori and group manifolds

$T^k$ has the $k$ commuting Killing vectors $\partial_{y^m}$ and gauge group $U(1)^k$; a group manifold $G$ has
$2\dim G$ Killing vectors, the left- and right-invariant fields of @sec-maurer-cartan, and gauge group $G \times
G$; a coset $G/H$ has the $\dim G$ Killing vectors of $G$ acting on the left [@duff1994, p. 14]. The number of
gauge fields is $\dim G$, not the number of internal dimensions.
:::
::::

The first exercise recomputes the brackets and inner products of the sphere's Killing vectors in the chart. It is the
input for every later computation on $M_4 \times S^2$, so it is worth checking once by machine.

::: {#exr-s2-killing-algebra}
#### The Killing algebra of the sphere

Verify the brackets and the inner products of the three Killing vectors with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-s2-killing-algebra >}}
:::

In the chart the Killing vectors look complicated, but in the ambient space they are the familiar rotation fields.
The second exercise pushes them forward to $\mathbb{R}^3$, as in the interactive figure, and rederives the brackets
from the cross product.

::: {#exr-nak-killing-cross-product}
#### The Killing vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$

Show that the push-forward of $K_a$ by the embedding $\vec n(\theta, \varphi)$ is $\vec e_a \times \vec n$. Writing
$\vec e_a \times \vec x = L_a\vec x$ with $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, use the bracket of linear vector fields,
$[L\vec x, M\vec x] = (ML - LM)\vec x$, to rederive $[K_a, K_b] = -\epsilon_{abc}K_c$, and compute $(\vec e_a \times \vec n)
\cdot (\vec e_b \times \vec n)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $K_3 = \partial_\varphi$ the push-forward is $\partial_\varphi\vec n = (-\sin\theta\sin\varphi, \sin\theta\cos\varphi, 0) =
\vec e_3 \times \vec n$; the other two follow in the same way. For linear fields $X = L\vec x$, $Y = M\vec x$, the
bracket $X^j\partial_jY - Y^j\partial_jX$ is $ML\vec x - LM\vec x$; since $[L_a, L_b] = \epsilon_{abc}L_c$ as matrices, the
fields have the opposite bracket $-\epsilon_{abc}$, the sign that runs through this chapter. Finally $(\vec e_a \times
\vec n)\cdot(\vec e_b \times \vec n) = \delta_{ab}(\vec n\cdot\vec n) - n_an_b = \delta_{ab} - n_an_b$:

{{< sage exr-nak-killing-cross-product >}}
:::

The number of gauge fields depends on the isometry group, not on the dimension. The third exercise makes the
comparison for the internal spaces met so far and for the three-sphere in two of its guises.

::: {#exr-nonabelian-counting}
#### Counting

For the internal spaces $S^1$, $T^2$, $S^2$, $S^3 = SU(2)$ and $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$, give the number of internal
dimensions and the number of gauge fields.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S^1$: $1$ dimension, $1$ gauge field ($U(1)$); $T^2$: $2$ and $2$ ($U(1)^2$); $S^2 = SO(3)/SO(2)$: $2$ and $3$
($SO(3)$); $S^3$ as the group manifold $SU(2)$: $3$ dimensions and $6$ gauge fields ($SU(2) \times SU(2)$, the
left and right actions); $S^3 = SO(4)/SO(3)$: $3$ and $6$, the same space and the same isometry group $SO(4) \cong
(SU(2) \times SU(2))/\mathbb{Z}_2$ (@exm-coset-s3). The gauge group is the isometry group, whose dimension can
exceed that of the space [@duff1994, p. 14].
:::
::::

### The ansatz

With the Killing vectors in hand, the circle ansatz generalises by replacing $A_\mu\,dx^\mu$ in $dy + A_\mu dx^\mu$ by
the vector-valued one-form $K^m_aA^a_\mu dx^\mu$. The internal metric stays fixed, so that the only new fields are the
gauge fields, one for each Killing vector.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-nonabelian-ansatz}
#### Non-abelian Kaluza-Klein ansatz

The **non-abelian ansatz** on $M_4 \times M_k$ is
$$
d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}(x)\,dx^\mu dx^\nu - \gamma_{mn}(y)\left(dy^m + K^m_a(y)A^a_\mu(x)\,dx^\mu\right)\left(dy^n + K^n_b(y)A^b_\nu(x)\,dx^\nu\right),
$$ {#eq-nonabelian-ansatz}
with components $\hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} - \gamma_{mn}K^m_aK^n_bA^a_\mu A^b_\nu$, $\hat g_{\mu m} = -\gamma_{mn}K^n_aA^a_\mu$,
$\hat g_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$, that is $\hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} + h_{mn}K^m_aK^n_bA^a_\mu A^b_\nu$, $\hat g_{\mu m} = h_{mn}K^n_aA^a_\mu$,
$\hat g_{mn} = h_{mn}$ in terms of the internal block $h = -\gamma$ [@duff1994, eq. 27, with the signature converted;
@overduin1998, eq. 31]: one gauge field $A^a_\mu$ per Killing vector, the internal
metric fixed, and no scalars (the generalisation with $y$-dependent internal metric brings in the scalar
fields of @sec-kk-reduction, which Part V treats in its own way).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the sphere the mixed components can be written out from the three Killing vectors. They depend on the point of the
sphere, unlike the circle's $-\phi^2A_\mu$, and this dependence is what the next chapter has to cope with.

::: {#exm-ansatz-sphere-components}
#### On the sphere

With @exm-internal-sphere, $\hat g_{\mu\theta} = -K^\theta_aA^a_\mu = \sin\varphi A^1_\mu - \cos\varphi A^2_\mu$ and
$\hat g_{\mu\varphi} = -\sin^2\theta K^\varphi_aA^a_\mu = \sin\theta\cos\theta(\cos\varphi A^1_\mu + \sin\varphi A^2_\mu) - \sin^2\theta A^3_\mu$:
the three gauge fields enter through the three Killing vectors, with $\varphi$-dependent coefficients.
:::

Collecting the products $K^m_aA^a_\mu$ into a single matrix makes the structure of the ansatz plain. It is the block form
of Part III with the corner promoted from a number to a $k \times k$ matrix.

::: {#exm-ansatz-block}
#### In block form

With $B^m{}_\mu = K^m_aA^a_\mu$ and $h = -\gamma$ the metric is $\begin{pmatrix} g + B^ThB & B^Th \\ hB & h \end{pmatrix}$,
the block form of @exm-ansatz-matrix with the $1 \times 1$ corner $-\phi^2$ replaced by the $k \times k$ internal block
$h$ and the column $-\phi^2A$ by $hB$ (@prp-nonabelian-inverse).
:::

The one-forms in the brackets of the ansatz have a geometric meaning. They single out a horizontal direction at each
point of the product, which is the defining property of a connection on a bundle.

::: {#exm-ansatz-tilt}
#### The tilt as a connection

The one-forms $dy^m + K^m_aA^a_\mu dx^\mu$ vanish on the horizontal directions $\partial_\mu - K^m_aA^a_\mu\partial_m$: moving
along $x^\mu$ one is carried along the fibre by the isometry generated by $A^a_\mu K_a$ (@fig-s2-gauge-fields), a
connection on the bundle $M_4 \times S^2 \to M_4$ with structure group $SO(3)$ (@def-bundle-connection), as $A_\mu$
was a $U(1)$ connection in @exm-gauge-field-kk.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise expands the line element on the sphere and reads off its components. It also checks the
horizontal-vector statement of @exm-ansatz-tilt, which says that the four-dimensional metric is what remains along the
horizontal directions.

::: {#exr-nak-ansatz-components}
#### Reading off the components

Expand @eq-nonabelian-ansatz on $S^2$ with symbolic $g_{\mu\nu}$ and $A^a_\mu$ (two spacetime dimensions suffice),
compare with @exm-ansatz-sphere-components, and show that the horizontal vectors $e_\mu = \partial_\mu - B^m{}_\mu\partial_m$
are orthogonal to the fibre with $\hat g(e_\mu, e_\nu) = g_{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The components are half the second derivatives of $d\hat s^2$ with respect to the coordinate differentials. Since
$dy^m + B^m{}_\mu dx^\mu$ vanishes on $e_\mu$ and the internal term is the only one that sees $\partial_m$,
$\hat g(e_\mu, \partial_m) = 0$, and on $e_\mu$, $e_\nu$ only $g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu$ survives:

{{< sage exr-nak-ansatz-components >}}
:::

The ansatz must reduce to Part III for the circle. The second exercise checks the reduction component by component,
including the sign of the internal block.

::: {#exr-nak-ansatz-circle}
#### The circle limit

Take $k = 1$, $\gamma = \phi^2$ constant along the circle, one Killing vector $K = \partial_y$ ($K^y = 1$) and one gauge
field $A^1_\mu = A_\mu$. Show that @eq-nonabelian-ansatz becomes @eq-kk-ansatz and its components @eq-kk-components.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B^y{}_\mu = K^yA_\mu = A_\mu$, so $d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - \phi^2(dy + A_\mu dx^\mu)^2$, which is
@eq-kk-ansatz. The components are $\hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} - \phi^2A_\mu A_\nu$, $\hat g_{\mu y} = -\phi^2A_\mu$ and
$\hat g_{yy} = -\phi^2$, those of @eq-kk-components; the internal block $h = -\phi^2$ is negative, as it must be for
the signature $(+, -, -, -, -)$. The only feature of Part III that the non-abelian ansatz drops is the
$x$-dependence of $\phi$: here the internal metric is frozen.
:::

At a single point of the sphere the three gauge fields cannot all be seen, because only two Killing-vector
combinations are independent there. The third exercise shows that the full $y$-dependence nevertheless determines
all three fields.

::: {#exr-nak-ansatz-recover}
#### Recovering the gauge fields

Show that at the point $\vec n$ of the sphere $\hat g_{\mu m}$ does not change when $A^a_\mu \to A^a_\mu + \lambda_\mu n^a$,
but that $A^a_\mu = -\tfrac32\langle K^m_a\hat g_{\mu m}\rangle$, the average over the sphere, recovers the gauge fields
from the metric. Use $K_a\cdot K_b = \delta_{ab} - n_an_b$ and $\langle n_an_b\rangle = \tfrac13\delta_{ab}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat g_{\mu m} = -\gamma_{mn}K^n_aA^a_\mu$ and $n^aK_a = 0$ at $\vec n$ (@exr-s2-killing-algebra), so the shift along
$n^a$ is invisible at that point. Contracting with $K^m_b$ gives $K^m_b\hat g_{\mu m} = -(K_b\cdot K_a)A^a_\mu = -
(\delta_{ab} - n_an_b)A^a_\mu$, whose average over the sphere is $-(1 - \tfrac13)A^b_\mu = -\tfrac23A^b_\mu$. Hence
$A^b_\mu = -\tfrac32\langle K^m_b\hat g_{\mu m}\rangle$: the three gauge fields are encoded in how $\hat g_{\mu m}$ varies over
the sphere, not in its value at one point.
:::
::::

Inverting the ansatz is the first step of every curvature computation. The block structure makes the inverse as
simple as in Part III, and the definition records it together with the determinant.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-nonabelian-inverse}
#### Inverse of the non-abelian ansatz

The inverse of @eq-nonabelian-ansatz is
$$
\hat g^{\mu\nu} = g^{\mu\nu}, \qquad \hat g^{\mu m} = -g^{\mu\nu}B^m{}_\nu = -K^m_aA^{a\mu}, \qquad
\hat g^{mn} = h^{mn} + B^m{}_\mu g^{\mu\nu}B^n{}_\nu = -\gamma^{mn} + B^m{}_\mu g^{\mu\nu}B^n{}_\nu ,
$$ {#eq-nonabelian-inverse}
which reduces to @eq-kk-inverse for the circle (@prp-nonabelian-inverse); as there, $\det\hat g = \det g\det h =
(-1)^k\det g\det\gamma$, the mixing dropping out of the volume element $\sqrt{|\hat g|} = \sqrt{-g}\sqrt{\gamma}$
(@exr-nonabelian-inverse).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The inverse formula uses nothing about the sphere or about Killing vectors. It is an identity of block matrices, and
this is what makes a single proof cover every internal space.

::: {#exm-inverse-general}
#### For any blocks

The identity $\hat g\hat g^{-1} = 1$ is a statement about block matrices: it holds for any square matrices $g$, $h$
with inverses and any rectangular $B$, whatever the dimensions. It is therefore proved once, for every internal
space.
:::

For the circle the formula must give back the inverse of Part III. The corner entry is the one to compare, because it
is where the gauge field appears quadratically.

::: {#exm-inverse-circle-check}
#### The circle again

For $k = 1$, $h = -\phi^2$ and $B = A$, the corner entry $h^{-1} + Bg^{-1}B^T = -\phi^{-2} + A_\mu A^\mu$ of @eq-kk-inverse.
:::

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

$\hat g\hat g^{-1} = 1$ and $\det\hat g = \det g\det h = \det g\sin^2\theta$ (@exr-nonabelian-inverse).
:::

At special points of the sphere the inverse can be written down by hand. The second exercise uses a point where one
Killing vector vanishes, which shows how a gauge field can drop out locally.

::: {#exr-nak-inverse-equator}
#### The inverse at a point of the equator

At $\theta = \pi/2$, $\varphi = 0$ (the point $\vec n = (1, 0, 0)$) evaluate $K_1$, $K_2$, $K_3$, the matrix $B^m{}_\mu$ and
the internal block $\hat g^{mn}$ of @eq-nonabelian-inverse. Which gauge field does not appear?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At $\theta = \pi/2$, $\varphi = 0$: $\cot\theta = 0$, so $K_1 = -\sin 0\,\partial_\theta = 0$, $K_2 = \partial_\theta$ and $K_3 =
\partial_\varphi$. Hence $B^\theta{}_\mu = A^2_\mu$ and $B^\varphi{}_\mu = A^3_\mu$, and with $\gamma = 1$ at this point,
$\hat g^{\theta\theta} = -1 + A^2_\mu A^{2\mu}$, $\hat g^{\theta\varphi} = A^2_\mu A^{3\mu}$, $\hat g^{\varphi\varphi} = -1 +
A^3_\mu A^{3\mu}$, while $\hat g^{\mu\theta} = -A^{2\mu}$, $\hat g^{\mu\varphi} = -A^{3\mu}$. The field $A^1$, which rotates
about the axis through this point, is absent: $K_1$ has a fixed point there.
:::

The determinant formula controls the volume element and therefore the normalisation of every reduced action. The
third exercise derives it by row operations, without inverting anything.

::: {#exr-nak-inverse-volume}
#### The volume element

Show $\det\hat g = \det g\det h$ by subtracting $B^T$ times the lower block rows from the upper ones, and deduce
$\int d^4x\,d^ky\sqrt{|\hat g|} = V_k\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}$ with $V_k = \int d^ky\sqrt\gamma$; evaluate $V_2$ for the unit
sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The row operation (upper rows) $-$ $B^T \times$ (lower rows) replaces $\begin{pmatrix} g + B^ThB & B^Th \end{pmatrix}$ by
$\begin{pmatrix} g & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and does not change the determinant; the result is block lower triangular with
determinant $\det g\det h$. For $h = -\gamma$, $\det h = (-1)^k\det\gamma$, so $|\det\hat g| = |\det g|\det\gamma$ and
$\sqrt{|\hat g|} = \sqrt{-g}\sqrt\gamma$. The $y$-integral of $\sqrt\gamma$ is the volume $V_k$; for the unit sphere
$V_2 = \int_0^\pi\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\theta\,d\varphi\,d\theta = 4\pi$.
:::
::::

The inverse is a theorem about block matrices of arbitrary size and sign. It is stated once for all internal spaces,
with the circle entry of Part III as a corollary.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-nonabelian-inverse}
#### The block inverse

For matrices $g$, $g^{-1}$, $h$, $h^{-1}$ with $gg^{-1} = 1$, $hh^{-1} = 1$ and any $B$ (of any sizes and signs, so in
particular $h = -\gamma$), the block matrix
$\begin{pmatrix} g + B^ThB & B^Th \\ hB & h \end{pmatrix}$ has the inverse $\begin{pmatrix} g^{-1} & -g^{-1}B^T \\ -
Bg^{-1} & h^{-1} + Bg^{-1}B^T \end{pmatrix}$ on both sides.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proposition becomes transparent once the block matrix is factored into triangular pieces. The factorisation also
explains the determinant and is the matrix form of the horizontal-vertical split of @exm-ansatz-tilt.

::: {#exm-nak-inverse-ldu}
#### A triangular factorisation

With $L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ B & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, the ansatz is $\hat g = L^T\begin{pmatrix} g & 0 \\ 0 & h
\end{pmatrix}L$. Since $\det L = 1$ and $L^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -B & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, it follows that $\det\hat g
= \det g\det h$ and $\hat g^{-1} = L^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(g^{-1}, h^{-1})L^{-T}$, which multiplies out to the matrix of
@prp-nonabelian-inverse (@exr-nak-ldu-factorisation).
:::

The rows of $L$ are the components of the one-forms $dx^\mu$ and $dy^m + B^m{}_\mu dx^\mu$. In this adapted frame both the
metric and its inverse are block diagonal, which is the cleanest way to remember the inverse.

::: {#exm-nak-inverse-frame}
#### The adapted frame

In the coframe $(dx^\mu, \theta^m = dy^m + B^m{}_\mu dx^\mu)$ the metric is $g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu + h_{mn}\theta^m\theta^n$, and
in the dual frame $(e_\mu = \partial_\mu - B^m{}_\mu\partial_m, \partial_m)$ the inverse is $\hat g^{-1} = g^{\mu\nu}e_\mu \otimes e_\nu +
h^{mn}\partial_m \otimes \partial_n$. Expanding $e_\mu$ in the coordinate basis gives back @eq-nonabelian-inverse
(@exr-nak-inverse-frame).
:::

The proposition holds for any sign of $h$. That is why the switch of signature from $(-, +, \dots, +)$ to
$(+, -, \dots, -)$, which flips the internal block, did not touch the statement.

::: {#exm-nak-inverse-signs}
#### Signs do not matter

Replacing $h = -\gamma$ by $h = +\gamma$, or $g$ by $-g$, changes the entries of $\hat g$ and $\hat g^{-1}$ but not the
identity: the proof uses only $gg^{-1} = 1$, $hh^{-1} = 1$ and associativity. The block inverse is therefore the same
theorem in both signature conventions, and with $g = 1$, $h = 1$ it inverts $L^TL$, a matrix congruent to the identity
(@exm-nak-inverse-ldu).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the triangular factorisation with fully symbolic blocks. Sage multiplies out
$L^T\operatorname{diag}(g, h)L$ and the inverse product for generic symmetric $g$ and $h$.

::: {#exr-nak-ldu-factorisation}
#### The factorisation in Sage

Verify $\hat g = L^T\operatorname{diag}(g, h)L$, $\det\hat g = \det g\det h$ and $\hat g^{-1} = L^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(g^{-1},
h^{-1})L^{-T}$ for a symbolic symmetric $3 \times 3$ block $g$, $2 \times 2$ block $h$ and $2 \times 3$ block $B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-nak-ldu-factorisation >}}
:::

The second exercise derives the inverse from the adapted frame of @exm-nak-inverse-frame. It shows that the
formula for $\hat g^{mn}$ is nothing but the expansion of the horizontal vectors $e_\mu$.

::: {#exr-nak-inverse-frame}
#### The inverse from the frame

Show that $(e_\mu, \partial_m)$ is dual to $(dx^\mu, \theta^m)$, and expand $g^{\mu\nu}e_\mu \otimes e_\nu + h^{mn}\partial_m \otimes
\partial_n$ in the coordinate basis to obtain @eq-nonabelian-inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dx^\mu(e_\nu) = \delta^\mu_\nu$, $dx^\mu(\partial_m) = 0$, $\theta^m(e_\nu) = -B^m{}_\nu + B^m{}_\nu = 0$ and $\theta^m(\partial_n) = \delta^m_n$, so
the frames are dual; a metric diagonal in a coframe has an inverse diagonal in the dual frame, with inverted blocks.
Expanding, $g^{\mu\nu}(\partial_\mu - B^m{}_\mu\partial_m)(\partial_\nu - B^n{}_\nu\partial_n)$ contributes $g^{\mu\nu}$ to $\hat g^{\mu\nu}$,
$-g^{\mu\nu}B^m{}_\nu$ to $\hat g^{\mu m}$ and $B^m{}_\mu g^{\mu\nu}B^n{}_\nu$ to $\hat g^{mn}$, and $h^{mn}\partial_m\partial_n$ adds $h^{mn}$:
exactly @eq-nonabelian-inverse.
:::

On a flat torus the Killing vectors are the coordinate fields and the blocks are constant. The third exercise writes
the inverse for two gauge fields and checks one product by hand.

::: {#exr-nak-inverse-torus}
#### The torus

For $T^2$ with constant metric $\gamma_{mn}$ and $K_a = \partial_a$ ($B^m{}_\mu = A^m_\mu$), write $\hat g$ and $\hat g^{-1}$
and check the entry $(\hat g\hat g^{-1})^\mu{}_m = 0$ directly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} - \gamma_{mn}A^m_\mu A^n_\nu$, $\hat g_{\mu m} = -\gamma_{mn}A^n_\mu$, $\hat g_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$, and
$\hat g^{\mu\nu} = g^{\mu\nu}$, $\hat g^{\mu m} = -A^{m\mu}$, $\hat g^{mn} = -\gamma^{mn} + A^m_\mu A^{n\mu}$. Then
$\hat g_{\mu\lambda}\hat g^{\lambda m} + \hat g_{\mu n}\hat g^{nm} = -(g_{\mu\lambda} - \gamma_{pq}A^p_\mu A^q_\lambda)A^{m\lambda} -
\gamma_{np}A^p_\mu(-\gamma^{nm} + A^n_\lambda A^{m\lambda}) = -A^m_\mu + \gamma_{pq}A^p_\mu A^q_\lambda A^{m\lambda} + A^m_\mu -
\gamma_{np}A^p_\mu A^n_\lambda A^{m\lambda} = 0$. Two Maxwell fields with a constant coupling matrix, the abelian case of
@exm-reduced-scalar-flat.
:::
::::

## The non-abelian gauge transformation {#sec-nonabelian-gauge}

The coordinate changes of the internal space along its Killing vectors, with parameters depending on spacetime,
preserve the form of the ansatz and act on the gauge fields as Yang-Mills gauge transformations, with the
structure constants of the isometry algebra. This section derives that transformation on the sphere, following
@duff1994 [Sec. 5, eqs. 29-30], and states it as an identity in the coordinates of the sphere and the jets of the
fields.

### Internal diffeomorphisms along Killing vectors

In Part III the gauge transformation was a shift of the circle coordinate by a function of spacetime. The
non-abelian analogue moves each fibre by an isometry, chosen independently at each spacetime point.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-killing-diffeomorphism}
#### Diffeomorphism along the Killing vectors

A **diffeomorphism along the Killing vectors** is the infinitesimal coordinate change
$$
x'^\mu = x^\mu, \qquad y'^m = y^m + \xi^m(x, y), \qquad \xi^m = \epsilon^a(x)K^m_a(y),
$$ {#eq-killing-shift}
with parameters $\epsilon^a(x)$ depending on spacetime only [@duff1994, eq. 29]: at each $x$ an isometry of the
internal space, varying from point to point. For the circle it is @eq-circle-shift with $K = \partial_y$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
If the parameters do not depend on spacetime, every fibre is moved by the same isometry. This is a symmetry of the
reduced theory of the familiar global kind, and it rotates the gauge fields among themselves.

::: {#exm-killing-shift-constant}
#### Constant parameters

$\epsilon^a$ constant: a rigid isometry of the fibre, the global $G$ symmetry of the reduced theory, which leaves
the ansatz invariant with $A^a_\mu$ rotated in the adjoint representation (@exm-nonabelian-adjoint-rotation).
:::

On the sphere the vector field $\xi$ is an infinitesimal rotation about the axis $\vec\epsilon(x)$. The figure
follows one point of the fibre as this axis changes along spacetime.

::: {#exm-killing-shift-sphere}
#### On the sphere

$\xi = \epsilon^1(x)K_1 + \epsilon^2(x)K_2 + \epsilon^3(x)K_3$: a rotation of the sphere by the angle vector
$\vec\epsilon(x)$, different at each spacetime point (@fig-nonabelian-gauge-rotation); the composition of two such
transformations is again one, with the Lie algebra of $SO(3)$ as composition law.
:::

The effect of the diffeomorphism on the metric is computed with the Lie derivative of Part I. The spacetime
dependence of $\xi$ is what makes the derivative terms appear.

::: {#exm-killing-shift-metric-variation}
#### The induced change of the metric

To first order the metric changes by the Lie derivative along $\xi$ (@def-lie-derivative), $\delta\hat g_{AB} =
\xi^C\partial_C\hat g_{AB} + \partial_A\xi^C\hat g_{CB} + \partial_B\xi^C\hat g_{AC}$ (@eq-lie-metric); since $\xi$ depends on $x$, the
terms $\partial_\mu\xi^m$ contribute, which is what generates $\partial_\mu\epsilon^a$ in the gauge transformation.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The non-abelian gauge transformation. Left: the same gray point of the sphere fibre relabelled by the rotation
$e^{\epsilon^a(x)K_a}$, with $\epsilon(x)$ varying along $x$. Right: for a parameter $\epsilon^3(x)$ acting on a constant
$A^1$, the induced $\delta A^3 = \partial_x\epsilon^3$ and the commutator term $\delta A^2 = \epsilon_{132}A^1\epsilon^3 = -A^1
\epsilon^3$, which generates a new component. The identity $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu m} = K_{mc}\,\delta A^c_\mu$ is checked
symbolically. Generated by
`figures/nonabelian_gauge_rotation.sage`.](figures/nonabelian_gauge_rotation.svg){#fig-nonabelian-gauge-rotation width=100%}

The first exercise compares the diffeomorphism with its circle counterpart. It also settles a sign that is easy to get
wrong: the Lie derivative and the relabelling of coordinates differ by the sign of the parameter.

::: {#exr-nak-shift-circle}
#### Relabelling versus dragging

For the circle, $\xi = \epsilon(x)\partial_y$. Compute $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu y}$ for @eq-kk-components and compare with the
change $A'_\mu = A_\mu - \partial_\mu\epsilon$ of @eq-kk-gauge under the relabelling $y' = y + \epsilon$. Explain the relative sign.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only the term $\partial_\mu\xi^y\hat g_{yy} = -\phi^2\partial_\mu\epsilon$ survives ($\hat g$ does not depend on $y$ and
$\partial_y\xi^y = 0$), so $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu y} = -\phi^2\partial_\mu\epsilon$, which is the change of $\hat g_{\mu y} = -\phi^2A_\mu$
under $A_\mu \to A_\mu + \partial_\mu\epsilon$. Under the relabelling $x' = x + \xi$ the new components, compared at the same
coordinate values, are $\hat g'_{AB} = \hat g_{AB} - (\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g)_{AB}$ to first order: the Lie derivative describes
the active transformation, equivalently the relabelling by $-\xi$. Both are gauge transformations, with parameters
$\epsilon$ and $-\epsilon$; this chapter uses the Lie derivative throughout.
:::

Two isometries applied in different orders differ by a third, and so do the gauge transformations they induce. The
second exercise computes this composition law at fixed spacetime point.

::: {#exr-nonabelian-algebra-closure}
#### Closure

Show that two transformations @eq-killing-shift with parameters $\epsilon_1$, $\epsilon_2$ compose to one with
parameter $\epsilon_3^c = f_{ab}{}^c\epsilon_1^a\epsilon_2^b$ to second order, using $[K_a, K_b] = f_{ab}{}^cK_c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The commutator of the vector fields $\xi_1 = \epsilon_1^aK_a$ and $\xi_2 = \epsilon_2^bK_b$ at fixed $x$ is
$\epsilon_1^a\epsilon_2^b[K_a, K_b] = f_{ab}{}^c\epsilon_1^a\epsilon_2^b\,K_c$, again along the Killing vectors: the
transformations form a group, the gauge group of the reduced theory, with the Lie algebra of $G$. The
$x$-derivatives of the parameters add the inhomogeneous terms that make the composition law that of a local
symmetry (@def-global-local-symmetry).
:::

The third exercise looks at finite rotations instead of infinitesimal ones. The group commutator of two rotations is,
to second order, a rotation about the third axis, the finite form of the closure just found.

::: {#exr-nak-group-commutator}
#### The group commutator of two rotations

With $R_a(s) = e^{sL_a}$, $(L_a)_{bc} = -\epsilon_{abc}$, the flow of $K_a$ on $\vec n$ (@exr-nak-killing-cross-product),
compute $R_1(s)R_2(t)R_1(-s)R_2(-t)$ to second order in $s$, $t$ and identify the result.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding each exponential to second order, the terms of order $s$, $t$, $s^2$, $t^2$ cancel and what remains is
$1 + st[L_1, L_2] = 1 + stL_3$, the rotation by the angle $st$ about the third axis. The matrices obey $[L_a, L_b] =
\epsilon_{abc}L_c$; the vector fields they generate, $L_a\vec n$, have the opposite bracket (@exr-nak-killing-cross-product):

{{< sage exr-nak-group-commutator >}}
:::
::::

### The gauge transformation

Applying the Lie derivative to the mixed components of the ansatz gives the transformation of the gauge fields. The
definition states the result for any internal space; the proposition below proves it on the sphere.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-nonabelian-kk-gauge-transformation}
#### The induced gauge transformation

Under @eq-killing-shift the ansatz @eq-nonabelian-ansatz keeps its form, with $g$ and $h$ unchanged and
$$
\delta A^c_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon^c - f_{ab}{}^cA^a_\mu\epsilon^b ,
$$ {#eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge}
where $f_{ab}{}^c$ are the structure constants of the Killing vectors, $[K_a, K_b] = f_{ab}{}^cK_c$ [@duff1994, eq.
30]. Here $\delta\hat g = \mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g$ is the change under the diffeomorphism generated by $\xi$
(@exm-killing-shift-metric-variation); read as a relabelling of coordinates, the components change by $-\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g$,
which amounts to $\epsilon \to -\epsilon$ and gives $A' = A - \partial\epsilon$ of @eq-kk-gauge for the circle (@exr-nak-shift-circle).
For the sphere, $f_{ab}{}^c = -\epsilon_{abc}$ and $\delta A^c_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon^c + \epsilon_{abc}A^a_\mu\epsilon^b$
(@prp-nonabelian-gauge): the infinitesimal Yang-Mills transformation of @def-nonabelian-gauge-field, whose gauge
group is the isometry group $SO(3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The derivation is a short computation with the Lie derivative. Its key step uses that the Killing vectors preserve
the internal metric, so that the Lie derivative of a lowered Killing vector is again a combination of Killing vectors.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-derivation}
#### The derivation

$\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu m} = \xi^n\partial_n\hat g_{\mu m} + \partial_m\xi^n\hat g_{\mu n} + \partial_\mu\xi^nh_{nm}$ with $\hat g_{\mu m} =
K_{ma}A^a_\mu$ ($K_{ma} = h_{mn}K^n_a$, $h = -\gamma$; every term is linear in $h$, so the sign of the internal block
drops out): the last term is $K_{ma}\partial_\mu\epsilon^a$, and the first two are $\epsilon^bA^a_\mu
(\mathcal{L}_{K_b}K_a)_m$, the Lie derivative of the covector $K_{ma}$ along $K_b$, which equals $h_{mn}[K_b, K_a]^n =
f_{ba}{}^cK_{mc}$ because $\mathcal{L}_{K_b}h = 0$. Hence $\delta\hat g_{\mu m} = K_{mc}(\partial_\mu\epsilon^c + f_{ba}{}^c\epsilon^bA^a_\mu)$,
which is @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge (@exr-nonabelian-gauge).
:::

The internal block of the ansatz must not change, or the form of the ansatz would not be preserved. That it does not
is exactly the Killing property of the vectors along which the fibres are moved.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-internal-block}
#### The internal block is unchanged

$\mathcal{L}_\xi h_{mn} = \epsilon^a\mathcal{L}_{K_a}h_{mn} = 0$ because the $K_a$ are Killing (@prp-sphere-killing): the
internal metric, and with it the size and shape of the sphere, is not a gauge degree of freedom.
:::

For constant parameters the derivative term disappears and only the commutator term is left. It rotates the three
gauge fields into each other like the components of a vector in three dimensions.

::: {#exm-nonabelian-adjoint-rotation}
#### The commutator term

For constant $\epsilon$, $\delta A^c = -f_{ab}{}^cA^a\epsilon^b$ is the adjoint action (@def-adjoint): on the sphere
$\delta A^c = \epsilon_{abc}A^a\epsilon^b$, that is $\delta\vec A = \vec A \times \vec\epsilon = -\vec\epsilon \times \vec A$, a rotation
of the three gauge fields into each other, as in @exm-nonabelian-su2. The right panel of @fig-nonabelian-gauge-rotation
shows $\epsilon^3$ turning $A^1$ into $-A^2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the Sage version of @exm-nonabelian-derivation. It computes the Lie derivative of the mixed
components on the sphere with symbolic gauge fields and parameters.

::: {#exr-nonabelian-gauge}
#### The Lie derivative of the mixed component

Compute $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu m}$ for $\xi = \epsilon^a(x)K_a$ on the sphere and read off $\delta A^c_\mu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-nonabelian-gauge >}}
:::

A gauge transformation is only useful if the field strength transforms covariantly. The second exercise checks this
for the transformation the geometry produced, with arbitrary functions as fields and parameters.

::: {#exr-nak-field-strength-covariance}
#### Covariance of the field strength

With $F^c_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A^c_\nu - \partial_\nu A^c_\mu + \epsilon_{abc}A^a_\mu A^b_\nu$, show that @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge on the sphere
gives $\delta F^c = \epsilon_{abc}F^a\epsilon^b$, and hence that $F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu}$ is gauge invariant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The derivative terms give $\epsilon_{abc}(\partial_\mu A^a_\nu - \partial_\nu A^a_\mu)\epsilon^b$ plus terms with $\partial\epsilon$; the latter
cancel against the variation of the commutator term with $\delta A = \partial\epsilon$, and the remaining quadratic terms combine
by the Jacobi identity into $\epsilon_{abc}\epsilon_{dea}A^d_\mu A^e_\nu\epsilon^b$. So $\delta\vec F = \vec F \times \vec\epsilon$, a rotation,
and $\delta(\vec F\cdot\vec F) = 2\vec F\cdot(\vec F \times \vec\epsilon) = 0$:

{{< sage exr-nak-field-strength-covariance >}}
:::

The spacetime block $\hat g_{\mu\nu}$ also contains the gauge fields, through the Killing inner products. The third
exercise checks, for a rigid rotation, that its change is entirely accounted for by the rotation of the gauge fields.

::: {#exr-nak-inner-product-covariance}
#### The spacetime block

For constant $\epsilon$, show $K_b(K_a\cdot K_c) = f_{ba}{}^d\,K_d\cdot K_c + f_{bc}{}^d\,K_a\cdot K_d$ and deduce that
$\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu\nu}$ equals the change of $h_{mn}B^m{}_\mu B^n{}_\nu$ under $\delta A^a = -f_{de}{}^aA^d\epsilon^e$, so that
$g_{\mu\nu}$ is invariant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\mathcal{L}_{K_b}h = 0$, $K_b(h(K_a, K_c)) = h([K_b, K_a], K_c) + h(K_a, [K_b, K_c])$, which is the identity with $[K_b,
K_a] = f_{ba}{}^dK_d$. For constant $\epsilon$, $\partial_\mu\xi = 0$, so $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu\nu} = \epsilon^bK_b(h(K_a, K_c))A^a_\mu
A^c_\nu = \epsilon^b(f_{ba}{}^dh(K_d, K_c) + f_{bc}{}^dh(K_a, K_d))A^a_\mu A^c_\nu$. On the other side, $\delta(h(K_a, K_c)A^aA^c) =
h(K_a, K_c)(\delta A^aA^c + A^a\delta A^c)$ with $\delta A^a = -f_{de}{}^aA^d\epsilon^e = f_{ed}{}^a\epsilon^eA^d$; renaming indices, the
two expressions agree. Hence $\delta g_{\mu\nu} = \delta\hat g_{\mu\nu} - \delta(h_{mn}B^mB^n) = 0$.
:::
::::

The structure constants of the gauge theory are not chosen; they are read off from the internal geometry. The next
definition records this, and the examples sort out the sign relative to the Killing brackets.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-structure-constants-from-killing}
#### Structure constants of the gauge group

The **structure constants** of the reduced gauge theory are those of the Killing algebra of the internal space,
$f_{ab}{}^c$ in $[K_a, K_b] = f_{ab}{}^cK_c$ (@def-coset-structure-constants for cosets): the gauge group is the
isometry group $G$ of $M_k$, "a subgroup of the $D$-dimensional general coordinate group" [@duff1994, p. 16].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the sphere the Killing brackets carry a minus sign, and the gauge transformation carries the opposite sign. The
example explains where this comes from and why it is harmless.

::: {#exm-structure-sphere}
#### $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ from the sphere

$f_{ab}{}^c = -\epsilon_{abc}$ from @eq-killing-brackets, so the gauge transformation @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge has
structure constants $-f_{ab}{}^c = +\epsilon_{abc}$: the vector fields generating a left action of a group represent its
Lie algebra with the opposite bracket (@exr-nak-killing-cross-product, @exr-nak-group-commutator), and the gauge
algebra they induce is that of the rotation matrices themselves. The sign is a convention for the orientation of the
generators, and $K_a \to -K_a$ gives $+\epsilon_{abc}$ with $A^a \to -A^a$: the field strength and the action are
unchanged (@exr-nonabelian-sign).
:::

When the isometries commute the commutator term disappears. A flat torus therefore gives several copies of Maxwell
theory and nothing non-abelian, however many dimensions it has.

::: {#exm-structure-torus}
#### Abelian limits

For $T^k$ the Killing vectors commute, $f = 0$, and @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge is $k$ copies of @eq-kk-gauge (with
$\epsilon \to -\epsilon$, @exr-nak-shift-circle); the non-abelian structure needs non-commuting isometries, which a flat
torus does not have.
:::

On a coset space two groups play a role, the group acting and the isotropy group of a point. Only the first one
becomes the gauge group of this ansatz.

::: {#exm-structure-coset}
#### Cosets and their isotropy

For $G/H$ the Killing vectors of the left action give the full $G$, and the gauge group of the reduction is $G$,
while the isotropy group $H$ (@def-isotropy-representation) is what the fields at a point of the fibre are charged
under: the two roles that $SO(3)$ and $SO(2)$ play in the CSDR constraints of Part V.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise shows that the sign of the structure constants is a matter of orientation. Flipping all Killing
vectors and all gauge fields together leaves the ansatz and the action unchanged.

::: {#exr-nonabelian-sign}
#### Sign conventions

Show that $K_a \to -K_a$ changes $f_{ab}{}^c \to -f_{ab}{}^c$ and that, with $A^a \to -A^a$, the field strength
$F^c = dA^c - \tfrac12f_{ab}{}^cA^a\wedge A^b$ of the gauge transformation @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge changes by an
overall sign only.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[-K_a, -K_b] = [K_a, K_b] = f_{ab}{}^cK_c = -f_{ab}{}^c(-K_c)$, so the constants of $-K$ are $-f$. The ansatz contains
$K^m_aA^a$, unchanged under the simultaneous flip; $F^c \to -dA^c - \tfrac12(-f)(-A)(-A) = -(dA^c - \tfrac12f_{ab}{}^cA^aA^b)$,
and $F^aF^a$, hence the Yang-Mills action, is invariant. The sign of $\epsilon_{abc}$ in @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge is
therefore a convention tied to the orientation of the Killing vectors.
:::

Not every set of numbers $f_{ab}{}^c$ is a set of structure constants, and not every Lie algebra gives a sensible
Yang-Mills theory. The second exercise checks the Jacobi identity and the sign of the Killing form for the sphere.

::: {#exr-nak-killing-form}
#### Jacobi identity and Killing form

For $f_{ab}{}^c = -\epsilon_{abc}$ and for the gauge constants $+\epsilon_{abc}$, verify the Jacobi identity
$f_{ab}{}^df_{dc}{}^e + \text{cyclic} = 0$ and compute the Killing form $B_{ab} = f_{ac}{}^df_{bd}{}^c$. Why does its
sign matter for the Yang-Mills action?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both sign choices satisfy the Jacobi identity, which is quadratic in $f$, and give $B_{ab} = -\epsilon_{acd}\epsilon_{bcd} = -
2\delta_{ab}$, which is quadratic as well. A negative-definite Killing form characterises the Lie algebra of a compact
semisimple group; it provides the positive invariant metric $\delta_{ab}$ on the algebra with which $F^aF^a$ is built,
so that the energy of the Yang-Mills field is positive:

{{< sage exr-nak-killing-form >}}
:::

A group manifold has two commuting sets of Killing vectors, from the left and from the right actions. The third
exercise works out the resulting structure constants, which split into two blocks.

::: {#exr-nak-group-manifold-algebra}
#### Two commuting algebras

On a group manifold $G$ with bi-invariant metric, let $\xi_a$ be the right-invariant fields (generating left
translations) and $e_a$ the left-invariant ones (@def-left-invariant-field). Show that $[e_a, \xi_b] = 0$ and that the
structure constants of the $2\dim G$ Killing vectors are block diagonal. What are the gauge group and the number of
gauge fields for $G = SU(2)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The flow of $e_a$ is right multiplication $g \mapsto ge^{tT_a}$, and the flow of $\xi_b$ is left multiplication $g \mapsto
e^{sT_b}g$; left and right multiplications commute, so the flows commute and $[e_a, \xi_b] = 0$. The $e_a$ close among
themselves with the constants of $\mathfrak{g}$, the $\xi_a$ with the opposite constants (they generate a left action,
@exm-structure-sphere), and there are no mixed brackets. For $SU(2) = S^3$ the gauge group is $SU(2) \times SU(2)$,
locally $SO(4)$, with six gauge fields (@exr-nonabelian-counting).
:::
::::

The general derivation is now specialised to the sphere and stated as an identity in the angles and the jets of the
fields. The proposition is the core of this section.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-nonabelian-gauge}
#### The gauge transformation on the sphere

For the ansatz on $M_4 \times S^2$ with the Killing vectors of @eq-sphere-killing and fixed $\mu$, the first-order
change of $\hat g_{\mu m}$ under @eq-killing-shift equals $\sum_ch_{mn}K^n_c(\partial_\mu\epsilon^c + \sum_{a,b}
\epsilon_{abc}A^a_\mu\epsilon^b)$ on the chart domain $\sin\theta \neq 0$ (both sides are linear in the internal metric, so
the identity may be stated with the round metric $\gamma_{mn}$ in place of $h_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$), as an identity in $(\theta, \varphi)$ and the
symbols $A^a_\mu$, $\epsilon^a$, $\partial_\mu\epsilon^a$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.NonAbelianKK.Gauge.gauge_transformation`, stated with the round metric $\gamma_{mn}$.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.NonAbelianKK.Gauge.gauge_transformation >}}

**Sage.** Checked symbolically in `figures/nonabelian_gauge_rotation.sage`, @exr-nonabelian-gauge and
@exr-nak-sphere-radius-r.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest instance of the proposition is a rotation about one axis. Only the third parameter is switched on, and
the formula separates into a shift of one gauge field and a rotation of the other two.

::: {#exm-nak-gauge-axis}
#### A rotation about the third axis

For $\epsilon = (0, 0, \epsilon^3(x))$: $\delta A^3_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon^3$, $\delta A^1_\mu = \epsilon_{231}A^2_\mu\epsilon^3 = A^2_\mu\epsilon^3$
and $\delta A^2_\mu = \epsilon_{132}A^1_\mu\epsilon^3 = -A^1_\mu\epsilon^3$. The field $A^3$ transforms like the photon of Part III,
while $(A^1, A^2)$ is rotated by the angle $-\epsilon^3$: the charged pair of the $U(1)$ generated by $K_3$
(@fig-nonabelian-gauge-rotation).
:::

Starting from the vacuum $A = 0$ the commutator term is absent. The gauge transformations then generate the pure-gauge
configurations, which are the infinitesimal versions of $g^{-1}\partial g$.

::: {#exm-nak-gauge-pure}
#### Pure gauge

For $A = 0$, $\delta A^c_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon^c$: the metric $g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - \gamma_{mn}(dy^m + \partial_\mu\epsilon^aK^m_adx^\mu)(dy^n +
\partial_\nu\epsilon^bK^n_bdx^\nu)$ is, to first order, the product metric in disguise, obtained from it by the diffeomorphism
@eq-killing-shift; its field strength vanishes, $F^c = d(d\epsilon^c) = 0$ to first order.
:::

The proposition is stated on the chart domain, because two of the Killing vectors contain $\cot\theta$. The identity
nevertheless holds on the whole sphere, as the Cartesian form of the Killing vectors shows.

::: {#exm-nak-gauge-poles}
#### The poles

$K_1$ and $K_2$ involve $\cot\theta$ and the chart $(\theta, \varphi)$ breaks down at the poles, which is why the proposition
assumes $\sin\theta \neq 0$. In Cartesian form $K_a = \vec e_a \times \vec n$ (@exr-nak-killing-cross-product) the Killing
vectors are smooth everywhere, both sides of the identity are smooth tensors, and equality on the dense chart domain
extends to the whole sphere by continuity.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Two gauge transformations applied in different orders differ by a third. The first exercise computes the commutator
on the gauge fields and identifies its parameter, the field-theoretic version of @exr-nonabelian-algebra-closure.

::: {#exr-nak-gauge-commutator}
#### The commutator of two gauge transformations

With $\delta_\epsilon A^c = \partial\epsilon^c + \epsilon_{abc}A^a\epsilon^b$, compute $[\delta_1, \delta_2]A = \delta_1(\delta_2A) - \delta_2(\delta_1A)$
for parameters $\epsilon_1$, $\epsilon_2$ depending on spacetime, and show that it is $\delta_{\epsilon_3}A$ with $\epsilon_3 = \epsilon_1
\times \epsilon_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta_1$ acts on the $A$ inside $\delta_2A$: $\delta_1(\delta_2A^c) = \epsilon_{abc}(\partial\epsilon_1^a + \epsilon_{dea}A^d\epsilon_1^e)\epsilon_2^b$. In the
commutator the derivative terms give $\epsilon_{abc}(\partial\epsilon_1^a\epsilon_2^b + \epsilon_1^a\partial\epsilon_2^b) = \partial(\epsilon_1 \times \epsilon_2)^c$,
and the terms linear in $A$ combine by the Jacobi identity into $\epsilon_{abc}A^a(\epsilon_1 \times \epsilon_2)^b$:

{{< sage exr-nak-gauge-commutator >}}
:::

The transformation found here must be the one postulated in Part II. The second exercise matches the two, including
the structure constants and the generators.

::: {#exr-nak-gauge-part-ii}
#### Comparison with Yang-Mills theory

Compare @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge on the sphere with $\delta A^a_\mu = \partial_\mu\alpha^a + f_{bc}{}^aA^b_\mu\alpha^c$ of
@def-nonabelian-gauge-field. Which structure constants and which generators $T_a$ does the geometry select?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\alpha = \epsilon$, @def-nonabelian-gauge-field gives $\delta A^c = \partial\epsilon^c + f^{\text{gauge}}_{ab}{}^cA^a\epsilon^b$, and the
geometry gives $\delta A^c = \partial\epsilon^c + \epsilon_{abc}A^a\epsilon^b$; hence $f^{\text{gauge}}_{ab}{}^c = \epsilon_{abc} = -f_{ab}{}^c$.
These are the constants of the anti-Hermitian generators $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ of
@exm-nonabelian-su2, or of the rotation matrices $L_a$ of @exr-nak-group-commutator, $[L_a, L_b] = \epsilon_{abc}L_c$. The
field strength is then @eq-yang-mills-F with $f_{bc}{}^a = \epsilon_{bca}$.
:::

Infinitesimal rotations exponentiate to finite ones. The third exercise integrates the commutator term for a constant
parameter and finds the finite gauge transformation of the three fields.

::: {#exr-nak-gauge-finite}
#### A finite rotation of the gauge fields

For constant $\epsilon = \alpha\vec e_3$, integrate $\frac{d\vec A}{d\alpha} = \vec A \times \vec e_3$ from $\vec A(0) = \vec A_0$. What is
$\vec A(2\pi)$, and why does the answer make sense for $SO(3)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Componentwise $\dot A^1 = A^2$, $\dot A^2 = -A^1$, $\dot A^3 = 0$, so $A^1 + iA^2$ obeys $\frac{d}{d\alpha}(A^1 + iA^2) = -
i(A^1 + iA^2)$ and $A^1 + iA^2 = e^{-i\alpha}(A^1_0 + iA^2_0)$: a rotation by $-\alpha$ about the third axis, with $A^3$
fixed. At $\alpha = 2\pi$ the fields return to $\vec A_0$, as they must for a rotation by $2\pi$ in $SO(3)$, which is the
identity; the gauge fields are in the adjoint representation, which does not see the sign that distinguishes
$SU(2)$ from $SO(3)$ (@exm-adjoint-su2).
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-01-isometries-gauge-fields-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first integrative exercise runs through the whole chapter for a sphere of arbitrary radius. It checks how each
result scales and which ones do not depend on the size of the internal space at all.

::: {#exr-nak-sphere-radius-r}
#### The sphere of radius $r$

For $\gamma = r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$: (a) show that the $K_a$ of @eq-sphere-killing are still Killing and that
$K_a\cdot K_b = r^2(\delta_{ab} - n_an_b)$; (b) check the block inverse and $\det\hat g = r^4\sin^2\theta\det g$; (c) show that
@prp-nonabelian-gauge holds unchanged. Which structure constants does the gauge group have?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\mathcal{L}_K(r^2\gamma_1) = r^2\mathcal{L}_K\gamma_1$ for the unit metric $\gamma_1$, so Killing vectors do not depend on the radius,
and inner products scale with $r^2$. (b) $\det h = r^4\sin^2\theta$ for $k = 2$. (c) Both sides of the identity are linear
in $h$, so the factor $r^2$ cancels: the gauge transformation, and with it the structure constants $\epsilon_{abc}$, are
independent of the radius, which will enter only the gauge coupling (@exr-nonabelian-coupling):

{{< sage exr-nak-sphere-radius-r >}}
:::

The second integrative exercise collects the circle limits of the chapter. Each formula must reduce to its Part III
counterpart, and the comparison fixes the sign conventions once and for all.

::: {#exr-nak-circle-limit}
#### Back to the circle

For $M_k = S^1$ with $\gamma = \phi^2$ constant and $K = \partial_y$, reduce @eq-nonabelian-ansatz, @eq-nonabelian-inverse,
@eq-killing-shift and @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge, and compare each with @eq-kk-ansatz, @eq-kk-inverse, @eq-circle-shift and
@eq-kk-gauge.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The ansatz becomes @eq-kk-ansatz with constant $\phi$ (@exr-nak-ansatz-circle). With $B = A$, $h = -\phi^2$ the inverse
is $\hat g^{\mu\nu} = g^{\mu\nu}$, $\hat g^{\mu y} = -A^\mu$, $\hat g^{yy} = -\phi^{-2} + A_\mu A^\mu$, which is @eq-kk-inverse
(@exm-inverse-circle-check). @eq-killing-shift is $y' = y + \epsilon(x)$, the shift @eq-circle-shift. Since $f = 0$,
@eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge is $\delta A_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon$, the Lie-derivative form; read as the relabelling, the components
change by the opposite amount, $A' = A - \partial\epsilon$, which is @eq-kk-gauge (@exr-nak-shift-circle). Nothing in this
chapter is new for the circle except the language of Killing vectors.
:::

The third integrative exercise applies the chapter to the three-sphere as a group manifold. It combines the counting
of gauge fields, the ansatz and the structure constants of two commuting algebras.

::: {#exr-nak-s3-ansatz}
#### The three-sphere as a group

On $S^3 = SU(2)$ with the bi-invariant metric, use the left-invariant fields $e_a$ and right-invariant fields $\xi_a$
(@exr-nak-group-manifold-algebra) as the six Killing vectors. (a) Write the ansatz with gauge fields $A^a_\mu$ along
$\xi_a$ and $\tilde A^a_\mu$ along $e_a$. (b) Write the gauge transformations. (c) Show that the gauge fields
$\tilde A^a$ alone have constant inner products $e_a\cdot e_b = \delta_{ab}$ (unit-radius normalisation), while a pair $e_a$,
$\xi_b$ has a non-constant inner product.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - \gamma_{mn}(dy^m + (\xi^m_aA^a_\mu + e^m_a\tilde A^a_\mu)dx^\mu)(dy^n + (\dots)dx^\nu)$, six gauge
fields on a three-dimensional internal space. (b) Since $[e_a, \xi_b] = 0$, the structure constants are block diagonal
and @eq-nonabelian-kk-gauge splits into two independent $SU(2)$ transformations, $\delta A = \partial\epsilon + (\dots)A\epsilon$ and
$\delta\tilde A = \partial\tilde\epsilon + (\dots)\tilde A\tilde\epsilon$, with opposite signs of the commutator terms
(@exm-structure-sphere); the gauge group is $SU(2) \times SU(2)$. (c) The left-invariant fields are orthonormal at the
identity and the metric is left-invariant, so $e_a\cdot e_b$ is the same at every point. But $\xi_b(g) = \sum_c
\operatorname{Ad}(g^{-1})_{cb}e_c(g)$ with the adjoint matrix of @def-adjoint, so $e_a\cdot\xi_b = \operatorname{Ad}(g^{-1})_{ab}$ varies over the
group, and only the restriction to one of the two $SU(2)$ factors has constant inner products. This is the
group-manifold reduction of Part VI.
:::
::::
